title: Cyclist’s Vuelta a España 2026 predictions
content:
Cyclist
Cyclist’s Vuelta a España 2026 predictions

Yes, it’s the final Grand Tour of the year, the Vuelta a España, which starts in time-honoured fashion with an individual time-trial tomorrow in… er, Monaco.

And far be it for us to deliver spoilers via our equally time-honoured Grand Tour predictions, but the distinctly un-Spanish location for the Gran Salida seems far less predictable at this point than the likely overall winner of the race in three Sundays’ time in Granada. But what about the other jerseys? Do we think Pogačar’s dominance has reached the point where he’ll win the lot – even the youth competition? Read on to find out…

Pete Muir, editor

Pete was bang on with his Pogačar and Del Toro jersey calls at the Tour de France. We shouldn’t flatter him though. He dared to say that Netcompany Ineos would have a great race. Alas, they suffered their worst Tour in over a decade.

GC: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

You could almost hear the collective groan when Pogačar announced that he was riding the Vuelta, as the other hopefuls realised they’d be fighting for scraps. I suspect Pog will ride the race with an expression that says, ‘Sorry everyone, but just let me complete my Grand Tour winner’s jersey collection and I promise I won’t come back next year.’

More interesting is who will take second place, and my money’s on Mattias Skjelmose (Lidl-Trek), who looked on good form at the Tour and won’t be fighting for leadership honours with Juan Ayuso. 

Points: Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike)

Most sprinters will have looked at the profile of this year’s Vuelta and thought, ‘Screw that.’ The first flat stage doesn’t appear until week two and there are only five sprint days in total. Who wants to slog over mountains in 40°C heat for that? Mads Pedersen will look to double up with his points jersey from the Tour, but I reckon Visma-Lease a Bike will bank on Van Aert being able to get over the lumpy stuff better, and will be backing him to bring back a jersey now that Sep Kuss’s chances in the GC have gone up in smoke.

Mountains: Tobias Halland Johannessen (Uno-X)

Really, the likely outcome is that Pogačar scoops the mountains jersey as he engages in his own personal race that will take place just in front of the race that everyone else is involved in. But we live in hope – after all, he didn’t win the polka dots at the Tour. So let’s go for a rider in form, who enjoys getting in a break, on a team that’s having a good year. 

Youth: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos)

Sticking my neck out here, as my prediction of a good Tour for Ineos proved somewhat misguided (their top rider was Egan Bernal in 20th place, 1h 48min behind Pogačar). I’m not sure what Onley’s form is like since his crash in June, but he will feel the pressure to justify his whopping transfer fee from Picnic PostNL last year, and to build some anticipation ahead of next year’s Tour de France, when it will pass through his home patch of the Scottish borders.

Bonus: Pog to wear red from day one    

The opening 9.4km time-trial takes place in Pog’s tax-friendly backyard of Monaco. He’ll just pop down in time for his TT slot, wave to his neighbours on the way round, and then go home for dinner once he’s won the first stage. Then he’ll keep the red jersey for the following 20 stages.

Ewan Wilson, staff writer

I also called Pogačar and Del Toro’s podium runs at the Tour. That said, I also dared to say that Paula Blasi would win the women’s race. How wrong I was.

GC: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

Tadej Pogačar enters the Vuelta with all the subtlety of a brick through the window. Like a thief, he’s ready to gobble up every stage and spend evening after evening toasting to another day in the red jersey. You know what, he might even go into red on day one, given he knows the tax-free roads of Monaco like the back of his hand.

Points classification: Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek)

I promise you’re not having post-Tour déjà vu. I’m just starting to feel more confident in the fact that no one quite does a points classification like Mads Pedersen. I don’t need to search out reasons to justify this either. Pedersen hasn’t left a Grand Tour without a stage win or a green jersey since the 2024 Tour de France.

Mountains jersey: Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike)

Logic would suggest that Tadej Pogačar will sleepwalk into the polka-dots again, but the Vuelta favours the breakaway more than the Tour.

In the absence of a big GC leader, Visma’s A-list riders will be off the leash. If he wants to test out new waters, it seems obvious for Sepp Kuss to target the polka-dot jersey. It’s one of the few things missing in the American’s palmarès, and he’s certainly deserving of one.

Young rider: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos)

If Oscar Onley were a racehorse, you wouldn’t put a flutter anywhere near him. He’s DNFed three WorldTour races this year and he’s barely ridden since the spring. However, in his most recent appearance, the Scot bounced back to finish second at the Vuelta a Burgos. If he doesn’t come a cropper, a top ten is within reach.

Bonus prediction: Axel Laurence wins a stage

French rider Axel Laurence has picked up wins on the WorldTour and second division this year. After a year of success, it feels like this Vuelta is filled with stages suited to a rugged Laurence victory, so after a torrid Tour de France, Laurence will give Netcompany something to get their AI motherboards excited about.

Laurence Kilpatrick, staff writer

Laurence is the only writer on the team to make zero correct predictions at the Tour. Having learnt his lesson, he’s reined in his contrarian views.

GC: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

It’s not even worth joking that it will be anyone other than Tufty McGreedy wins in red at end of the Vuelta’s three weeks. Greatness: witness it, enjoy it, savour it and hope it will end very soon for the good of the sport.

Points: Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike)

I’m with Pete on this one. Pedersen is the clearest candidate, but I think there’s something in the air this year for WvA. The lingering improbability of that Roubaix win will give him enough wings (sorry) to get over the absurdly lumpy parcours and clear up the few sprint stages that have been tossed in.

Mountains: Richard Carapaz (EF Education–EasyPost)

Just when we thought he was out, he pulls himself back in. Old Richie has reinvented himself a number of times in his long career and after those exploits in the Tour de France, with the eyes of the globe watching, surely it’s worth chucking a few quid on a repeat. Plus it’s gonna be bloody hot and that’s sweat off a Carapaz’s back.

Youth: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos)

Sorry to be boring but it’s another vote for the Scotsman – if only because I’m desperate to have some British Isles interest in this Grand Tour. He’s been about as tasty on a bike this year as sheep intestines but a few shoots of recovery are clearly enough for the whole Cyclist office to think he’s suddenly hot to trot.

Bonus prediction: Stages shortened

Multiple stages to be drastically shortened because of extreme heat with maybe another stopped altogether thanks to a raging wildfire. Unpopular as they are, what this Vuelta could do with are a few more climate protestors. It’s getting urgent. Someone book them a plane ticket and a blank cheque for the super glue shop.

Robyn Davidson, web writer

Robyn nailed her GC and young rider predictions at the Tour de France (although maybe her Tour de France Femmes calls are better left unremembered). None of that really matters however, as she’s currently too heartbroken over Julian Alaphilippe’s retirement to care.

GC: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

Let’s be honest, he has one hand on the red jersey already. This will again be a Grand Tour dictated by Tadej Pogačar, who is set to be the first man since Jonas Vingegaard this season to join the club of winning all three Grand Tours. There’s no rival strong enough to pose a serious threat, which is a damn shame.

Points: Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek)

Mads Pedersen ‘will not specifically chase green’, according to sports director Maxime Monfort, however he’s targeting stage wins. Well, like a couple of good madison riders on the track, the two kind of go hand in hand. He arrives as defending points classification champion and off a summer that saw him win the jersey at the Tour too. He’s perfect for this type of parcours. There’s nary a flat day to be seen, lumps and bumps littered all about the place.

Mountains: Tadej Pogačar

The heart says Richard Carapaz. The head says this mountainous route has points-sweeper Pogačar written all over it as the other podium fighters battle it out between themselves, the red jersey a shrinking figure in the distance.

Young rider: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos)

It’s been a topsy turvy year for the Scotsman who, despite a strong finish at the Volta ao Algarve, was forced to miss the Tour de France after a spate of stage race abandonments and a dangle above a ravine at the Tour Auvergne – Rhône-Alpes. Things have been on the up through. Upon his return to the peloton he missed the top step of the Vuelta a Burgos podium by just five seconds to Felix Gall – who will also be at the start line of the Vuelta.

I pondered over Decathlon CMA CGM’s LéoBisiaux given his youth classification topping following a strong performance at the Vuelta a Burgos, but don’t reckon the 21-year-old has the steam just yet to last three weeks on top spot here.

Bonus prediction: Primož Roglič hunts the vibes classification

The Vuelta has played host to many a Primož Roglič triumph over the years that has the Slovenian tied for most overall victories. But now, things are different. His level doesn’t match that of Pogačar, and to make matters worse he was hit by a car driver that ruled him out of both the Clásica San Sebastián and Vuelta a Burgos in an unideal build-up to the race.

I get the vibe he won’t quite be there on GC. That gives us hope to see a stage-hunting attacking Roglič that reared its head at the Tour in 2025. Which might just land him atop another classification…

Martin James, production editor

You’d think getting to go last would give you an advantage. Then again, at least Martin managed to predict the Tour winner correctly in his last effort at the predictions game. ‘Cos nobody else got that one correct, right?

GC: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG)

I mean, obviously. What may be more interesting will be how many stage wins he picks up along the way, since total Grand Tour stage wins is one of very few areas where Pogačar is still (relatively) far down the all-time list (he currently sits 10th overall with just 35). Still, he’s just six away from the current sixth place, a certain B Hinault. And he wasn’t too bad, was he?

If you’re wondering, good ole’ Eddy is still quite a ways clear with 64.

Points: Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike)

When he’s actually been able to race this season, Van Aert’s form has been up there with the best of his career. A strong spring Classics campaign had us all looking forward to what Grand Tour season had in store for the Belgian… only for him to miss a scheduled appearance at the Tour de France due to the effects of an elbow injury. That means he’ll be not only relatively fresh coming into the Vuelta, but also very much determined to make his mark. And with his team not going into the race with any real GC ambitions (sorry, Sepp), Van Aert looks ideally placed to make amends for his withdrawal in the final week of the 2024 Vuelta, when he was leading both the points and mountains classifications.

Mountains: Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost)

Carapaz was excellent in the mountains in the Tour de France, winning two stages and finishing 60 points clear of Tadej Pogačar despite ending up a full 20 minutes down on GC. Which proves that A) Carapaz has little to no chance on GC at the Vuelta, and B) even a dominant overall winner doesn’t actually always win the mountains prize by default. Carapaz’s 1st-3rd-1st trio of stage finishes in the Alps late on at the Tour suggests that playing the long game for the mountains jersey is his best bet for winning one of the main prizes at the Vuelta, and may well see him sneak onto the podium on GC too.

Young rider: Jørgen Nordhagen (Visma-Lease a Bike)

What do you mean, why would a rider who was only the sixth best young rider at the Vuelta a Burgos earlier this month be the best one of all at the actual Vuelta? To be honest, after seeing an unbroken Oscar Onley love-in from everyone else, going for Nordhagen instead for the white jersey is as much about being different than anything else, but let’s face it, these young ‘uns are pretty good these days, And with Paul Seixas already locked in as the next Tadej Pogačar, we need another Dane to step up and claim the title of the next Jonas Vingegaard.

Bonus prediction: No Grand Tour hurrah for Primoz

I’m not going out of my way to delberately disagree with Robyn here – in fact, I’d love nothing more than for her to be right and for Primoz Roglič to at least feature regularly in stage-hunting action at the Vuelta. But sadly, I just don’t see Roglič achieving anything of note at all at the race where he’s achieved the most down the years. Roglič has every right to look back at team manoeuvrings across his career – both at Visma and his current team Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe – as having robbed him of more success, but it’s hard to escape the fact that what was always a late start in road cycling has now hastened what feels like a premature finish. Roglič is a five-time Grand Tour winner – one of only 12 men to have acheived that – but I have a feeling that this might be the last time the original Slovenian Grand Tour superstar lines up for a three-week stage race.

Will Strickson, website editor

*Shh don’t tell anyone, I’ve rushed back from holiday to sneak my predictions in when no one’s looking. That should leave me with five easy wins right? Ha. Cue the music.

Red: Oscar Onley

It’s optimistic, but I’m banking on Tadej Pogačar only coming to the race to be at the start at his home in Monaco. He’ll win a stage or two then duck out to prepare for Worlds and leaving Fausto Coppi behind as the solo all-time leader in Lombardia wins – which he needs to secure before Paul Seixas steps up another level.

With Pogačar gone, this race becomes far and away the best men’s Grand Tour of the year and the freshest of all riders rises to the top. Yes while my colleagues have boldly predicted Kelso’s finest to take the best young rider competition, I’m banking on OO to see off challenges from Felix Gall, Richard Carapaz and Enric Mas to take his first Grand Tour win.

Green: Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike)

It’s only Matthew Brennan’s first Grand Tour but he is going to come out a-swinging. With Mads Pedersen focusing on stage wins and helping Mattias Skjelmose, the door is wide open for the admittedly brutal points classification. With most of the peloton’s sprinters hiding in Belgium and Germany, Visma-Lease a Bike should be all over this, with Wout van Aert he’ll be able to go for his own success while helping the Stockton Rocket to green glory.

White: Oscar Onley

No danger.

Blue polka dots: Ben Tulett (Visma-Lease a Bike)

It’s taken all my energy not to take the Jay Vine defence, and I’m frankly shocked Laurence didn’t, but we have a job to do here.

It’s going to be a good three weeks for Visma, despite not having a proper GC leader (unless Kuss decides he’s back in the game). With half the team taking a chunk of stage wins, they’re going to be racing on the front the whole time, and the Sevenoaks Stallion will be getting himself up there on the climbs to bring the mountains jersey home.

Bonus: Josh Tarling wins at least one stage

Josh Tarling is a warrior. Following the death of his brother Fin just over a week ago, Josh has decided to still ride the Vuelta and there’s no doubt that he is going to be more motivated than ever to win. Whether it’s on the opening prologue or later in the race, he ended the Tour de France in fine form and I’m confident he’ll take that to another level here. I think he’ll take a pair of stages and there won’t be a dry eye in the house. And even if he doesn’t, chapeau Josh.

Reminder that you can donate in Fin Tarling’s memory to helping the next generation of Welsh cyclists on this Gofundme.
